svg.aria-label: Soap from wood-ash lye. Principle: fat + alkali → soap + glycerol (saponification). Safety first: lye is a strongly corrosive liquid; wear goggles (lye splashed in the eyes can cause blindness), gloves and long sleeves, work outdoors or somewhere well ventilated, keep children and pets away, and have a large bucket of clean water beside you; use stainless steel, enamel, ceramic, wooden or heat-resistant plastic containers, not aluminium pans (they react with the alkali, giving off hydrogen, and corrode right through); on the skin rinse at once under plenty of running water and do not neutralise with vinegar; in the eyes hold the eyelids open and rinse continuously under running water, then get medical help; if swallowed do not make the person vomit, call 120 at once. 1 Making lye: a bucket with small holes in the bottom, gravel then straw in the bottom, filled with fine white or pale grey hardwood ash; pour in rainwater or soft water that has been boiled and cooled slowly; the brown liquid that drips out is the lye; pour it back over the ash several times to make it stronger; do not use ash from painted wood, plastic, rubbish or coal. 2 Testing the strength: put in a fresh egg or a piece of potato; if it sinks the lye is too weak, boil it down over a low heat; if it floats with about a coin-sized patch showing the strength is right; if it floats too high it is too strong, add a little water. 3 Preparing the fat: boil the fat with an equal amount of water and when cool take the clean fat that sets on top. 4 Cooking: melt the fat over a low heat, slowly add the lye while stirring, starting with about as much lye as fat; keep it just bubbling over a low heat and keep stirring for several hours until it thickens like thin porridge or honey. 5 Checking it is done: a drop on a cold plate sets into a soft lump, and a little stirred into clean water dissolves with no oil floating; oil floating means not enough alkali, add more lye and keep cooking; the result is a brown, paste-like soft soap. 6 Optional, harden with salt: add a large handful of salt while hot, the soap floats to the top, scoop it into a mould and cut when cool. 7 Curing: 2-6 weeks in a dry, airy place. 8 Testing (you must do this): pH 9-10 is right, above 11 means too much alkali; only use it on your hands if the back-of-hand test gives no stinging and no redness; do not taste it with your tongue
svg.title: Soap from wood-ash lye

Wood-ash lye is mainly potassium carbonate and potassium hydroxide, so it makes soft soap (a paste).
It is not as hard as shop soap, but you use it in exactly the same way.
